engineering_justification: The supply type sets the input level (about 56 V or 12 V); the INA238 reads up to 85 V.
I = P / V for the single INA238 at the sign input.
Second term of I = P / V.
The energy counter integrates input power, so its hourly increase is the hour's mean power.
The CPU+GPU+CV rail is fed from the module input (VDD_IN), so it is part of module power.
DeepStream inference runs on the GPU and CPU; load-based DVFS raises their rail power.
Video decode, scaling and memory traffic load the SOC rail, which is in module power but not in CPU+GPU power.
Die temperature = surrounding air + thermal resistance x dissipated power (NVIDIA Thermal Design Guide).
NVIDIA's thermal model uses total module power as the heat load; SOC, memory and regulator heat also reach the die.
The air around the passive heat sink sets the baseline die temperature.
CPU and GPU sensors sit on the same die; CPU is primary because the GPU sensor fails (-256) when the GPU is power-gated.
GPU inference heats the GPU area more than the CPU area, widening the GPU-CPU gap.
board_temp is the INA238 die temperature, which TI says tracks the local (system) ambient.
Conversion losses on the same board warm the INA238 die.
Module power is part of sign input power if the module is fed through the INA238.
Modem power rises with uplink traffic and transmit power.
Downlink traffic also costs modem power, less per byte than uplink.
A 56 V sign may have an extra conversion stage with its own losses.
A thermostat heater would switch on in the cold.
A hygrostat heater would switch on when humid.
The display brightness may follow the light sensor.
device_power may be a copy of an INA3221 rail.
Sun on the enclosure warms the board.
